ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Regional disparities of States 
 
 *121. SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR:† 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the regional disparities of different States are widening; 
(b) whether as per statistics prepared by the Central Statistical 
Organisation, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal 
together account for 42.5 per cent of aggregate State domestic product, while 
Orissa, Bihar and a few other States' share has far declined in 2003-04 at 1993-94 
price level; 
(c) whether it is because of the fact  that the new economic policy of 
Government hardly had the scope for practicising welfare economics in these 
backward and poverty-stricken States; and 
(d) if so, what is the action plan of Government to address this issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Tenth Five Year Plan document (Para 1.29, Chapter I, Volume 
I, Tenth Five Year Plan 2002-07) and Mid-Term Appraisal of Tenth Five Year 
Plan (Para 18.2 of Chapter 18) recognize the growing regional disparities. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Ms. Pramila Bohidar. 

RAJYA SABHA [1 December, 2005] 
(b) As latest statistics provided by the Central Statistical Organisation, 
Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal together account 
for 42.76% of all India Gross Domestic Product in 2003-04 at constant 1 993-
94 prices. The share of Orissa, Bihar and other States in the all-India GDP for 
the years 2001-02 to 2003-04 are provided in the Statement-I (See below). 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. On the contrary, the new economic policy of 
Government, with its emphasis on more inclusive growth, has enhanced the scope 
for social and economic development in the backward States. A substantial 
increase in the resources transferred from the Central Government has been guaranteed 
through the acceptance of the award of the Twelfth Finance Commission. The 
implementation of the National Employment Guarantee Act, under which the 
wage component payable to unskilled workers w ill be met entirely by the 
Central Government, will result in direct benefits for people below the poverty line 
in backward areas. The significant increase in funding for the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan, 
the launch of the National Rural Health Mission and the Bharat Nirman 
Programmes have all been designed to help States to step up expenditures in the social 
and infrastructure sectors. A cooked Mid-Day Meals Scheme, fully funded by the 
Central Government, for all primary schools has been implemented since September, 
2004. In addition, the Rashtriya Shra m Vikas Yojana (RSVY) that was 
designed to ensure special focus on b ackward districts has been enlarged, 
strengthened and subsumed into the new Backward Regions Grants Fund. In 
addition to overall growth targets for the country, the Tenth Five Year Plan has also 
specified State-wise growth rate targets with a view to encourage introspection at 
the State level as well as to serve as a catalyst to reinvigorate planning at the State 
level.

What is the Government of India's action plan to tackle this issue? 
SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Sir, I would like to inform the hon. Member that the UPA 
Government has taken a number of steps to address this problem not only in Orissa but also 
in other backward regions of the country. Now, I would like to share some of the information 
with the hon. Member. As far as the reasons for backwardness are concerned, these could 
be geographical location, lack of natural resources, poor governance and delivery 
system. These are the main reasons for re gional disparity. Redressal of regional 
imbalance is an integral component of every Five Year Plan. The hon. Member, I am sure, 
must have gone through the Midterm Appraisal of the Tenth Plan Document, where 
particularly the Tenth Five Year Plan has adopted the following approaches to resolve the 
regional disparity issues under the Mid-term Appraisal. They are (i) Identify the 
backward areas and target them with add itional resources; (ii) Improve overall 
environment for economic growth in less developed States through infrastructure, 
institutional reforms and incentive structures. Sir, Orissa figures as one of the backward 
States in the country. That is why a number of schemes have been undertaken. To address these 
problems pertaining to backward regions of the country, the Central Government helps in 
the process of regional development through weightage in the formula used for the distribution 
of Central assistance and the Special Area Programme that is there, namely, the RSV. In 
fact, the hon. Member would happy to know that nearly 8-10 districts are covered under 
this scheme in the State of Orissa. There are other special programmes which are being 
addressed to take care of the backwardness of the States. No. 1 is the Backward 
Region Grant Fund. As the hon. Member knows, an announcement has been made 
by the hon. Finance Minister, during the Budget Session, providing Rs. 5,000 crores, 
particularly for this year alone, namely, 2005-06. Then, there are a number of other 
programmes which have been specially targeted... 
MR. CHAIRMAN: The details may be circulated amongst the hon. Members.

Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) Based on the first five rounds of talks between the Special 
Representatives of India and China on the boundary question, both sides signed 
the "Agreement on Political Parameters and Guiding Principles for Settlement of 
India-China Boundary Question" on April 11,2005 during the visit of the Chinese 
Premier Wen Jiabao to India. The sixth round of talks between the Special 
Representatives was held in Beijing from September 26 to September 28, 2005, 
which marked the beginning of the second phase of negotiations. In the second 
phase of negotiations, the two Special Representatives are mandated to work out an 
agreed framework for a boundary settlement on the basis of the aforementioned 
Agreement. Such an agreed framework will provide the basis for the delineation 
and demarcation of the India-China boundary to be subsequently undertaken by 
civil and military officials and surveyors of the two sides.

question.

Kumar Sanghi.

SAARC Summit 
*126. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Indian delegation led by the Prime Minister participated in the 
13th SAARC Summit held on 12th November, 2005 in Dhaka; 
(b) if so, the detail of discussions/outcome of decisions taken at the said 
meeting; 
(c) whether the Indian delegation put forward before the SAARC meeting any 
specific suggestions; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of member nations to India's suggestion for a united bid to 
combat terrorism with "zero tolerance" towards cross-border terror? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) to (d) Yes, Sir. The Indian delegation led by the Prime Minister 
participated in the Thirteenth SAARC Summit held on November 12-13, 2005 
in Dhaka. 
The Summit had an exhaustive agenda. India participated actively in the 
deliberations at Dhaka and the Summit Declaration incorporates many of the new 
proposals made by India. The outcome of the Summit is in consonance with 
India's objectives and provides new opportunities to further the process of regional 
economic integration in South Asia. 
India had taken a strong initiative which ensured the entry of Afghanistan as a 
new member of SAARC. With Afghanistan's entry, SAARC would acquire a 
more complete regional identity. 
The Summit noted the renewed interest of other regional and international 
organizations, bodies and entities to cooperate with SAARC in fields of mutual 
interest. India has welcomed the interest shown by China as well as Japan to be 
associated with SAARC as observers, and would welcome similar association 
with other interested countries as well. It has been agreed that the SAARC 
Council of Ministers will decide the modalities in this regard. 
The Summit was notable for the signing of three very important trade 
facilitation agreements namely: 
*  The Agreement on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Customs 
Matters 
22 

[1 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
* The Agreement on the Establishment of SAARC Arbitration Council 
* The Limited Agreement on Avoidance of Double Taxation and Mutual 
Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters. 
India's offer for hosting the SAARC Ce ntre for Disaster Management and 
Preparedness has been accepted by the Summit. The extensive loss of life and property due 
to natural disasters such as the Tsunami and earthquakes, which affected the region during 
the past one year, led to the clear recognition of the need for a permanent regional response 
mechanism and India's record and demonstrated capabilities led to acceptance of our proposal 
to host the Centre in India, closely associated with the National Institute for Disaster 
Management in Delhi. 
India has long argued that if South Asia is to become a dynamic component of the 
larger process of regional cooperation and globalization that is taken place in the world, it must 
first bring about economic integration amongst the member countries, as an essential pre-
requisite. In this context, India offered, on a reciprocal basis, transit facilities to all countries 
of the region and also greater air connectivity through a virtual open skies arrangement. 
India took the lead in favour of there being no delay in the operationalisation of the SAFTA 
(South Asia Free Trade Area) Agreement. 
The proposal made by India for setting up a South Asia University as a centre of 
excellence was welcomed. 
The Summit has also noted other important proposals made by India, such as the setting 
up a Regional Food Bank, establishing a SAARC Museum of Textiles and Handicrafts, a 
Regional Tele-Medicine Network, and the holding of a SAARC Car Rally. 
A major theme at the Summit was cooperation in counter terrorism. There is a 
strong condemnation of terrorism in the Summit Declaration and a renewed 
commitment to eliminate this scourge. For the first time, there is also a clear reference to 
avoiding double standards in tackling this challenge. This is a major achievement of the 
Summit, and is in line with India's own foreign policy objectives.

Support of UN Resolution on Iran 
*137. SHRI S. S. AHLUWALIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government supported in September 2005, the resolutioh to 
restrict nuclear programmes of Iran; 
(b) if so, the details of the resolution, including its sponsors and other 
member countries who voted for and against the said resolution and those 
abstained from voting; 
(c) the rationale behind the stand taken by India; 
(d) whether stand of Government is undergoing revision; and 
(e) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNALAFFAIRS 
(SHRI RAO INDERJIT SINGH): (a) to (e) The IAEA Board of Governors has been 
discussing the issue of Iran's nuclear programme, its compliance with its 
Treaty obligations and its Safeguard Agreement with the IAEA for more than 
two years. Iran had in an agreement with the EU-3 (France, Germany, UK) in 
November 2004 agreed to suspend on a voluntary basis all enrichment related and 
reprocessing activities. On 1 August 2005, Iran gave a notification that it would 
resume uranium conversion activities at the Uranium Conversion Facility 
(UCF) at Isfahan. The IAEA Board of Governors adopted a resolution by 
consensus on 11 August 2005 which inter-alia urged Iran to re-establish full 
suspension of all activities at the UCF. 
The matter was discussed at the IAEA Board of Governors meeting held 
from September 19-24,2005. EU-3 moved a resolution on the issue, which inter-
alia found Iran in non-compliance with its safeguards obligations and urged Iran to 
implement the necessary confidence building and transparency measures 
including suspension of all enrichment related activity. It did not include a 
referral of the matter to the UNSC but requested DG, IAEA to continue his efforts 
to implement the resolutions on Iran and to report again to the Board. 
Twenty two States voted in favour of the resolution which was adopted by the 
IAEA Board. These were Argentina, Au stralia, Belgium, Canada, Ecuador, 
France, Germany, Ghana, Hungary, India,  Italy, Japan, Republic of Korea, 
Netherlands, Peru, Poland, Portugal, Singapore, Slovenia, 
38 

[1 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Sweden, UK, and USA. Twelve states abstained namely Algeria, Brazil, China, Mexico, 
Algeria, Nigeria, Pakistan, Russia, Sri Lanka, South Africa, Tunisia, Vietnam and Yemen. 
Venezuela voted against the resolution. 
India voted in favour of the resolution since the resolution took account of our concern 
against not referring the matter to the UN Security Council and providing more time for 
negotiations. India's vote was in keeping with our consistent stance that more time should be 
given for resolution of the issue through negotiations within the framework of the IAEA. 
The consistent approach of the Government has been that this matter should be resolved 
in the IAEA, and to this end has maintained regular communication with all parties 
concerned. The issue was discussed at the IAEA Board meeting on 24 November 2005. 
The Board reiterated its support for the resumption of negotiations between Iran and EU-
3. No resolution was presented to the Board. 
The Indian statement noted stated that Iran had been more forthcoming in providing 
additional access to the IAEA since September 2005 Board meeting. The present 
situation offered vital diplomatic space, which confirmed India's position that this 
matter should be resolved within the IAEA and that enough time and cooperation should be 
given to the IAEA to complete its work.

Statement 
Brief on Trai's Recommendations on Growth of Telecom Services In 
Rural India 
The recommendations of TRAI provide for a higher quantitative and 
qualitative growth in telecom services in the country, particularly in rural areas. 
Since tele-density is interlinked with the level of development, the large 
differential between rural (1.94%) and ur ban tele-density (31.1%) cannot be 
sustainable. The recommendations state that without focus on rural areas, 
sizeable growth in telecom sector would not be possible. 
As per the TRAI's recommendations, the present USO Policy of 
subsidizing individual DELs, VPTs, MARR replacement, PTICs/HPTICs 
would barely be able to achieve rural tele-density targets of 4% by 2010 even-
after giving huge subsidy support of around Rs. 30,000 crores. 
65 

RAJYA SABHA [1 December, 2005] 
Recommendations state that such low tele-density in rural areas in 2010 and high 
subsidies to achieve so little can not be acceptable therefore there is a need for 
a relook at traditional policies regarding the communication needs of rural 
areas and to change these to "Universal Service Opportunity" rather than a 
"Universal Service Obligation". 
TRAI has further recognized so me features of the Indian rural market, viz. 
substantial purchasing power at the right price, expansion of broadband/ Internet 
service provided by private sector and the immense popularity of cable TV in 
India and that such connections are far in excess of fixed line telephones —a 
unique feature in the world. It recommends that the proposed policy should look at 
this feature and encourage triple - play networks which can be facilitated by 
Unified Licensing Regime, already recommended by the Authority to the 
Government. 
The Authority has recommended that  an alternative approach of 
facilitating network infrastructure expa nsion should be adopted. This 
approach proposes to offer financial incentives to service providers in the form of 
coverage of partial cost of shared in frastructure and license fee and spectrum 
charge reduction based on the number of rural base station locations. If the 
proposed scheme is implemented early then TRAI's experience of mobile 
growth in urban areas indicate that India would achieve rural tele-density of around 
15% by December, 2007 and this combined with expected urban tele-density 
of around 43% would take the overall tele-density to 22.98% easily meeting the 
target of 250 million subscribers set out by the Hon'ble Minister of 
Communications & IT. If the present USO Policy continues then TRAI expects 
that India would achieve rural tele-density of only around 3% by 2007 end and 
in order to achieve the subscriber base target of 250 million it would require an 
urban tele-density of 70% by December, 2007 which is too ambitious a target for 
urban areas and even if achieved would create a much larger rural/urban divide, 
which cannot be an acceptable policy. 
TRAI has noted that there are already contractual commitments in the present 
USO policy. Accordingly it recommends that during the validity of these 
agreements both the schemes may work in parallel as there would be balances in 
USOF to fund both, but ultimately only the network infrastructure expansion 
approach should be followed for providing support from the USOF. 
The salient features of TRAI's recommendations are as follows:— 
66 

[1 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
• Sharing of infrastructure to receive support from USO. 
• Supporting backbone infrastructure through USO fund 
• Discount in Annual License Fee and Spectrum Charge linked M Rural 
Coverage. 
• Development of suitable applications. 
• Reduction of rural VSAT license fees and spectrum charges and 
provision of transponders at affordable rates. 
• No right of way charges for networks in rural areas. 
• Niche Operators to be supported from USOF and exemption from 
spectrum charges. 
• No spectrum fees for usage of CorDECT and similar technologies in 
rural areas as well as for usage of 450 MHz. 
• No prior SACFA clearance for deployment of towers upto 40 m. in rural 
areas. 
• Funds collected as Universal Access levy should be made available to 
USOF.

Subject: Enhancement of the Foreign Direct Investment ceiling from 49 per 
cent to 74 per cent in the Telecom sector. 
Government of India 
Ministry of Commerce & Industry 
Department of Industrial Policy & Promotion 
Secretariat for Industrial Assistance 
PRESS NOTE NO. 5 (2005 SERIES) 
1. In pursuance of the Government's commitment to liberalise the FDI 
regime, it has been decided to enhance the Foreign Direct Investment ceiling 
from 49 per cent to 74 per cent in certain telecom services [ such as Basic, 
Cellular, Unified Access Services, National/lnternatioanl Long Distance, V-Sat, 
Public Mobile Radio Trunked Services (PMRTS), Global Mobile Personal 
Communications Services (GMPCS) and other value added services], subject 
to the following conditions:- 
A. The total composite foreign holding including but not limited to 
investments by Foreign Institutional Investors (Flls), Non-Resident 
Indians (NRIs), Foreign Currency Convertible Bonds (FCCBs), 
American Depository Receipts (ADRs), Global Depository Receipts 
(GDRs), convertible preference shares, proportionate foreign 
investment in Indian promoters/investment companies including their 
holding companies, etc., hereinafter referred as FDI, will not exceed 
74 per cent. Thus, 74 per cent foreign investment can be made 
directly or indirectly in the operating company or through a holding 
company. Hence, the remaining 26 per cent will be owned by 
resident Indian citizens or an Indian Company (i.e. foreign direct 
investment does not exceed 49 per cent and the management is with the 
Indian owners). It is clarified that proportionate foreign component of 
such an Indian Company will also be counted towards the ceiling of 74%. 
However, foreign component in the total holding of Indian public sector 
banks and Indian public sector financial institutions will be treated as 
'Indian' holding. The licensee will be required to disclose the status of such 
foreign holding and certify that the foreign investment is within the 
ceiling of 74% on a half yearly basis. 
80 

[1 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
B. The majority Directors on the Board including Chairman, Managing 
Director and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) shall be resident Indian 
citizens, enforced through licence agreement. The appointment 
to these positions from among resident Indian citizens shall be 
made in consultation with serious I ndian investors. Serious investor 
has been defined below in para G (ii). 
C. The Share Holder Agreements (S HA) shall specifically incorporate 
the condition that majority directors on the Board including 
Chairman, Managing Director and CEO shall be resident Indian 
citizens and shall also envisage the conditions of adherence to 
Licence Agreement. 
D. FDI upto 49 per cent will continue to be on automatic route. 
Foreign Investment Promotion Board (FIPB) approval shall be 
required for FDI in the licens ee company/Indian promoters/ 
investment companies including their holding companies if it has 
a bearing on the overall ceiling of 74 per cent. While approving the 
investment proposals, FIPB shall take note that investment is 
not coming from unfriendly countries. 
E. The investment approval by FIPB shall envisage the conditionality 
that Company would adhere to licence Agreement. 
F. FDI shall be subject to laws of India and not the laws of the foreign 
country/countries. 
G. Department of Telecommunications (DoT) will enforce the above 
and the conditions mentioned below through appropriate 
amendment in licence:- 
(i) There shall be a non-obstante cl ause in the licence which confers 
powers upon the licensor to cancel the licence under certain 
defined circumstances. 
(ii) In order to ensure that at leas t one serious resident Indian promoter 
subscribes reasonable amount of the resident Indian shareholding, 
such resident Indian promoter shall hold at least 10 per cent equity 
of the licensee company. 
(iii) The Company shall acknowledge compliance with the licence 
agreement as a part of Memorandum of Association of the 
Company. Any violation of the licence agreement shall 
automatically lead to the company being unable to carry on its 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [1 December, 2005] 
business in this regard. The duty to comply with the licence 
agreement shall also be made a part of Articles of Association. 
(iv) Chief Technical Officer (CTO) Chief Finance Officer (CFO) shall be 
resident Indian Citizens. The Licensor/DoT shall also be 
empowered to notify key positions to be held by resident Indian 
citizens. 
(v) The Company shall not transfer the following to any person/ place 
outside India:— 
(a) any accounting information relating to subscriber (except for 
roaming/billing) (Note: it does not restrict a statutorily required 
disclosure of financial nature); 
(b) user information (except pertaining to foreign subscribers using 
Indian Operator's network while roaming); and 
(c) details of their infrastructure/network diagram except to 
telecom equipment suppliers/manufacturers who undertake the 
installation, commissioning etc. of the infrastructure of the 
licensee company on signing of non-disclosure agreement. 
(vi) The company when entering into roaming agreements with service 
providers outside India must provide, on demand, the list of such 
users (telephone numbers, in case of foreign subscribers using 
Indian Operator's network while roaming). 
(vii) The Company must provide traceable identity of their subscribers. 
However, in case of providing service to roaming subscriber of 
foreign companies, the Indian Company shall endeavour to obtain 
traceable identity of roaming subscribers from the foreign company 
as a part of its roaming agreement. 
(viii) No traffic (mobile and landline) from subscribers within India to 
subscribers within India shall be hauled to any palce outside India. 
(ix) No Remote Access (RA) shall be provided to any equipment 
manufacturer or any other agency outside the country for any 
maintenance/repair by the licensee. However, RA may be allowed 
for catastrophic software failure (such as failure to boot up etc.) which 
would lead to major part of the network becoming 
82 

[1 December, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
non-functional for a prolonged period, subject to meeting the 
following conditions:— 
(a) An identified Government agency (Intelligence Bureau) will 
be notified, when RA is to be provided. 
(b) Remote Access password is to be enabled for a definite period 
only and only for access from pre-approved locations of the 
Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) Vendors and only 
for the equipments specifically under repair/maintenance. 
(c) The control of Remote Access i.e. activation, transfer of data 
termination etc. shall be within the country and not at a 
Remote location, abroad. 
(d) The Government agency will be given all support to record the 
transactions for on-line monitoring. 
(e) Any equipment or software that forms part the overall 
monitoring shall not be permitted to have remote access under 
any circumstances. 
(f) DoT will define appropriately the terms catastrophic software 
failure, major part of the network, and prolonged period used 
under this clause. 
(x) It shall be open to the Department of Telecommunications to restrict 
the licensee company from operating in any sensitive area from the 
national security angle. 
(xi) In order to maintain the privacy of voice and data, monitoring shall 
only be upon authorization by the Union Home Secretary or Home 
Secretaries of the States/Union Territories. 
(xii) For monitoring traffic, the li censee company shall provide blind 
access of their network and other facilities as well as to books of 
accounts to the security agencies. 
(xiii) In case of not adhering to licence contions envisaged in para G. the 
licence(s) granted to the company shall be deemed as cancelled and 
the licensor shall have the right to encash the performance bank 
guarantee(s) and the licensor shall not be liable for loss of any 
kind.

2. The conditions at para 1 above shall also be applicable to the existing

3. The relevant provisions of FDI policy for "investment companies", as given

Requirement of IT software professionals 
924. SHRI DIPANKAR MUKHERJEE: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether NASSCOM has estimated requirement of 1.1 million IT 
software professionals by the year 2008; 
(b) if so, presently the number of  total employees and engineers (IT 
and non-IT related disciplines separately) in the IT sector of India; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the job assigned to engineers in IT sector can be 
done by other graduates also; and 
(d) if so, what would be the requirement of engineering degree/diploma holders (IT 
and non-IT related disciplines separately) in IT sector, year-wise till 2008. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMUNICATIONS AND 
INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) to (d) As per the 
estimates of NASSCOM, the total number of IT Software and Services (ITS) and IT 
enabled Services-Business Process Outsourcing (ITeS-BPO) professional employed

Agenda of the SAARC Summit 
948. SHRI S.ANBALAGAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
< 
(a) whether the Prime Minister attend ed the SAARC Summit at Dhaka, 
recently; 
(b) if so, the details thereof including the leaders of the other countries 
participated in the Summit; 
(c) the agenda of the Summit and the consensus arrived at the Summit; 
(d) the features of the joint declaration made at the end of the Summit; and 
(e) the view points put forth by India at the Summit and the response of other 
countries thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI E. AHMMED): (a) The Indian delegation, consisting of Prime Minister, 
Minister of State for External Affairs (EA), Foreign Secretary and other senior 
officials of the Government of India, took part in the Thirteenth SAARC Summit 
held in Dhaka on November 12-13,2005. 
(b) The King of Nepal, the Presidents of Maldives and Sri Lanka, and the 
Prime Ministers of Bangladesh, Bhutan and Pakistan also participated in the 
Summit. 
(c) to (e) The Summit had an exhaustive agenda. India participated actively 
in both the preparations for the Summit as well as in its deliberations at Dhaka. The 
Summit Declaration incorporates many of the new proposals made by India. The 
major achievements of the Summit are in consonance with India's objectives and 
provide new opportunities to further the process of regional economic integration 
in South-Asia. 
India had taken a strong initiative to ensure the entry of Afghanistan as a new 
member of SAARC. The consensus decision taken by the SAARC Heads of 
State and Government to welcome Afghanistan as SAARC's eighth member is 
a major success for Indian diplomacy. With Afghanistan's entry, SAARC would 
acquire a more complete regional identity, and a country with which India has 
traditionally close and friendly relations would become part of SAARC. 
110 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The Summit noted the renewed interest of other regional and international 
organizations, bodies and entities to cooperate with SAARC in fields of mutual 
interest. India has welcomed the interest shown by China as well as Japan to be 
associated with SAARC as Observers. We would welcome similar association 
with other interested countries as well. It has been agreed that the C ouncil of 
Ministers will decide the modalities in this regard in their meeting in July, 2006. 
The Summit was also notable for the signing of three very important trade 
facilitation agreements. These include: 
* The Agreement on Mutual Administrative Assistance in Customs 
Matters 
* The Agreement on the Establishment of SAARC Arbitration Council 
* The Limited Agreement on Avoidance of Double Taxation and 
Mutual Administrative Assistance in Tax Matters 
India's offer for hosting the SAARC Ce ntre for Disaster Management and 
Preparedness has been welcomed and acce pted by the Summit. This is an 
important development, considering the extensive loss of life and property due 
to natural disasters such as the Tsunami and earthquakes, which have 
affected our region during the past one year. There was a clear recognition that 
we need a permanent regional response mechanism dedicated to disaster 
preparedness, emergency relief and rehabilitation. India's record and 
demonstrated capabilities in this regard helped in ensuring the su ccess of our 
proposal to host the Centre in India. This Centre will be closely associated with the 
National Institute for Disaster Management in Delhi. 
India has long argued that if South Asia is to become a dynamic 
component of the larger process of regional cooperation and globalization that is 
taking place in the world, it must firs t bring about economic integration 
amongst the member countries, as an essential pre-requisite. India put forward a 
bold new vision of a SAARC, which is interconnected, where political divisions 
do not stand in the way of the free movement of peoples, goods and services, and 
ideas, across our region. In this context, India offered, on a reciprocal basis, transit 
facilities to all countries of the region and also greater air connectivity through 
a virtual open skies arrangement. India took the lead in drafting a strong 
political message that there should be no delay in the operationalisation of the 
SAFTA (South Asia Free Trade Area) Agreement. 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [1 DECEMBER, 2005] 
The proposal made by India for the setting up of a South Asia University that 
would bring together scholars, scientists and students from all over South Asia 
in a centre of excellence was welcomed enthusiastically. 
The Summit has also noted with appreciation some other important 
proposals made by India, such as the setting up of a Regional Food Bank, a 
Regional Tele-Medicine Network, setting up of SAARC Museum of Textiles and 
Handicrafts to preserve and foster this valuable legacy of handicrafts and 
textiles, and the holding of a SAARC Car Rally in the run up to the 14th 
SAARC Summit, which will be held in India in the first quarter of 2007. We 
intend to develop these ideas further in close consultation with our SAARC 
partners. 
A major theme at the Summit was cooperation in counter terrorism. There 
is a very strong condemnation of terrorism in the Summit Declaration and renewed 
commitment to eliminate this scourge, both from the region as well as from the 
world. For the first time, there is also a clear reference to avoid double standards 
in tackling this collective challenge. This is a major achievement of the 
Summit, and is entirely in line with India's own foreign policy objectives. 
The Summit was a landmark event, which took place as SAARC enters the 
third decade of its existence. There was a strong sentiment amongst member 
countries that the time had come for us to move from a phase of declaratory and 
consultative processes to more practical and collaborative processes. India is a 
very strong advocate of collaboration in regional projects, particularly in areas 
such as infrastructure, poverty alleviation and dealing with cross border 
challenges such as natural disasters, pandemics like HIV/AIDS and Avian Flu 
and terrorism in all its forms and manifestations. It is hoped that when India hosts 
the next SAARC Summit in the first quarter of 2007, the stage would have been set 
for a significant upgradation in regional cooperation within SAARC and the first 
steps would have been taken towards establishing a truly free trade area in South 
Asia.

EMPLOYMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government propose to bring changes in labour laws so 
as to accelerate economic pace in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have received any suggestions etc. in this regard from the 
National Manufacturing Competitive Council and other Organization; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; and 
(e) Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR AND EMPLOYMENT (SHRI K. 
CHANDRASEKHAR RAO): (a) and (b) With a view to making labour markets flexible, A 
"Discussion Paper" 'making labour market flexible' has been circulated among various 
stakeholders for eliciting their views. These, inter-alia, include: 
(i) amendment in the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 by 
placing certain activity in a separate schedule so that provision of Section 10 
may not apply to these, and by replacing the term "emergency" with the term 
"public interest" in Section 31 of the Act; and 
(ii) amendment in the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 by raising the number filter 
from 100 to 300 for applicability of chapter VB and raising the 
compensation ceiling payable to workers on retrenchment, and on closure 
of the establishment, from 15 days' average pay to 45 days' average pay for every 
completed year of continuous service or any part thereof in excess of six 
months subject to the condition that such retrenchment compensation shall not 
be less than 90 days of average wages; and by extending the applicability of 
Section 36B to all undertakings.

Early Warning System in Orissa 
994. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a)' whether Orissa is an island of natural disaster necessitating 
establishment of an early warning system; 
(b) whether Government are in the process of establishing Tsunami Early 
Warning System in the country; 
(c) if so, whether Chandipur in the district of Balasore in Orissa is the most 
appropriate place for installation of this warning system; 
(d) whether the Central Government would consider installation of 
Tsunami Early Warning System in the above place or some other suitable place in 
the State at the earliest; and 
(e) if so, the time-frame within which it would be done? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF SCIENCE AND 
TECHNOLOGY (SHRI KAPIL SIBAL): (a) Orissa coast is highly vulnerable 
154 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to the cyclonic storms, which is one of the major natural disasters, affecting the east 
coast of India. Keeping in view the vulnerability of th e state, a Cyclone 
Warning Centre (CWC) was established in Bhubaneswar in 1973 to cater to the 
needs of Orissa coast, which forms part of time-tested organization for 
monitoring and forecasting of Tropical Cyclones. For speedy communication of 
warning messages, about 35 satellite-based Cyclone Warning Dissemination 
Systems (CWDS) have been installed along Orissa coast through which warning 
can be directly sent to the people in the affected areas, in local language. 
(b) Yes, Sir. Government of India is in the process of setting up an Early 
Warning system for Tsuna mis and Storm Surges in the Indian Ocean. The 
Department of Ocean Development (DOD), Department of Science and 
Technology (DST)/lndia Meteorological Department (IMD), Department of 
Space (DoS) and CSIR Laboratories are the major agencies involved in this 
endeavour. DOD is the lead agency. 
(c) and (d) As part of the Early Warning system for Tsunamis and Storm 
surges, a centre would be set up at Indian Natural Centre for Ocean 
Information Services (INCOIS), Hyderabad on a 24x7 basis. The decision to 
locate the Tsunami Warning Centre at INCOIS, Hyderabad was taken as 
INCOIS is being developed as an Ocean Services Centre with a view to make 
optimal utilization of the in-house f acilities created at INCOIS including 
Satellite Oceanography/Satellite Communication. INCOIS is the agency of the 
Department of Ocean Development and is already providing advisories on 
Potential Fishing Zone and ocean state parameters. 
(e) The system is scheduled to be operational by September, 2007.

gruoup?

TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIYAPPA): (a) Yes, Sir.

1010. SHRIMATI S.G INDIRA: Will the Minister of SHIPPING ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government had decided to join 1998 
agreement on Global Technical Regulations for Motor Vehicles; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether it is a fact that the design specifications of vehicles do not have to 
be changed to meet country specific regulations; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIYAPPA): (a) and  (b) 
Yes, Sir. The Government of India has approved the proposal for India's joining 
the 1998 Agreement on Globai Technical Regulations (GTR) for Motor 
Vehicles, administered by WP-29-Worid Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle 
Regulations, a body of the Economic Commission of Europe of the United 
Nations (UN-ECE). The 1998 Agreement is a forum for establishment of 
Global Technical Regulation for wheeled Motor Vehicles, equipment and parts 
which can be fitted and/or used on wheeled vehicles. The objective of 1998 
Agreement is to codify the international best practices in safety, emission 
regulations, energy sources and theft prevention equipments into global 
regulations without any binding obligations for reciprocal rec ognition of 
certification by signatory countries. 
(c) and (d) Since the Global Techni cal Regulations are formed by 
harmonization of existing regulations pf contracting countries as well as by 
establishment of new regulations with the consensus of all contracting parties, 
vehicles manufactured with such design specifications would largely meet the 
specification of the contracting parties.

1017. SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: W ill the Minister of 
SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to improve and upgrade existing 
National Highways in the country to make them all weather proof, and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS 
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) and (b) The development and improvement of National 
Highways is a continuous process and the improvement projects are taken up based on the 
design and guidelines for National Highways to make the roads alt weather proof. The 
design principles and guidelines are so framed to provide (i) the road section at least one 
meter above the highest flood level/water table, (ii) adequate surface and sub-surface 
drainage measures including camber on the top of the pavement and (iii) bituminous or 
concrete pavements as top layer.

1025. SHRI B.K. HARIPRASAD: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether of late Indian flag ships are being detained in overseas ports on 
flimsy technical grounds under 'code 30' of the maritime manual; 
(b) whether such minor deficiencies under 'Code 30' attributed to the 
detention of Indian ships abroad, do not render the ship unseaworthy or. sub-
standard; and 
(c) whether according to international maritime industry, Indian flag-ships 
are house-kept much better than their foreign counterparts, if so, the reasons for 
this discrimination against Indian flagships by foreign port authorities? 
192 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS 
(SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Some Indian ships have been 
detained for deficiencies, which in view of the Maritime Administration could not 
be regarded as detainable deficiencies and did not render the ships substantially 
substandard or unseaworthy, to be subjected to detention. 
(c) The house keeping standards of Indian ships have improved due to 
sustained efforts in this direction over last 4 to 5 years. Memoranda of 
Understanding on Port State Control have devised target factors for ships for 
enhanced Port State Control Inspections on the basis of their age, past record of 
owners. Classification Societies and the flag states etc. Generally, the MOUs target 
the ships on the basis of ships coming into high factor and there is no 
discrimination reported on this ground.

Credit Linked Capital Subsidy 
1028. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have launched a scheme on Credit Linked Capital 
Subsidy;* 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the criteria fixed for getting assistance under the scheme; and 
(d) the number of SSI units in Andhra Pradesh benefited by the scheme? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD) (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme (CLCSS) for technology upgradation 
of Small Scale Industries was launched in October 2000. The Scheme has been revised 
with effect from September 29,2005. The revised Scheme aims at facilitating 
technology upgradation of small scale industries, including tiny, agro and rural 
industrial units, by providing 15 per cent upfront capital subsidy (12 per cent prior to 
29.9.2005) on institutional finance availed of by them for induction of well-established and 
improved technology in specified sub-sectors/ products approved under the scheme. The 
admissible capital subsidy under the revised scheme is calculated 
194 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
with reference to the purchase price of plant and machinery. The maximum limit of eligible 
loan for calculation of capital subsidy under this Scheme has also been raised from Rs. 
40 lakh to Rs. 100 lakh. 
(c) The revised guidelines prescribed for availing of subsidy under the 
CLCSS, inter alia, include the following: 
(i) Subsidy at the revised rate of 15 per cent of the eligible investment in plant and 
machinery under the Scheme is available only for those beneficiary units, 
where term loans have been sanctioned by the eligible Primary Lending 
Institutions on or after September 29,2005. 
(ii) Units availing of subsidy under the CLCSS cannot avail of any other subsidy 
for technology upgradation from Central/State/UT Government. However, cases 
covered under National Equity Fund Scheme, which are otherwise eligible 
under CLCSS, can be covered under this scheme. 
(iii) Units in the North Eastern Region which are availing of financial 
incentives/subsidy under any scheme of the Government in the region are also 
eligible for subsidy under the CLCSS. 
(IV) Replacement of existing equipment/technology with the same 
equipment/technology does not qualify for subsidy benefit under CLCSS. This 
Scheme is also not applicable to units upgrading their technology with 
second-hand machinery. 
(d) 74 SSI Unit in the State of Andhra Pradesh have so far availed of 
benefits under the CLCSS since its inception. 
Grouping of industries 
1029. PROF. R.B.S. VARMA: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) the rationale behind the latest policy of Government to group small scale industries 
with medium scale industries (SMEs), thereby hoping that small would 
automatically graduate to medium; 
(b) in what way Government presume that small scale industries would graduate to 
medium scale, by grouping the two categories together; 
(c) what incentives are small scale industries being given to graduate to medium scale; 
195 

RAJYA SABHA [1 DECEMBER, 2005] 
(d) what steps Government are taking to allay the fears of small scale 
manufacturers that this policy would allow the bigger industrialists to take away 
major benefits and incentives being given by Government; and 
(e) whether Government plan to review this policy? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCAL E INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) In the Small and Medium Enterprises Development (SMED) Bill, 
2005 introduced in the Lok Sabha during in its last Budget session, the concept 
of Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) has been proposed. The rationale 
behind grouping small and medium enterprises in the framework of the Bill 
is as follows:— 
(i) In his Budget speeches for 2004-05 and 2005-06, the Finance Minister 
has referred to the need for adopting the concept of small and medium 
enterprises. 
(ii) The Department related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, in its 153rd report on the demands for grants (2004-05), 
endorsed inter alia the growing feeling that "India should also adopt the 
SME concept". 
(iii) Globally, small and medium enterprises are treated as a continuum. 
(iv) Small and medium enterprises have more in common with each other 
than either have with large enterprises and, hence, the need to provide a 
common legal framework for them. 
(v) In a dynamic economy as ours, some small enterprises do grow into 
medium enterprises overtime. 
(b) The Central Government is of the view that a common legal framwork (as in 
the SMED Bill) and the policy and programmes initiatives to flow therefrom 
may help small enterprises to grow into medium enterprises overtime. 
(c) Though promotion and development of small enterprises, including small 
scale industries, is the primary responsibility of State Government/ Union 
Territory (UT) Administrations, the Central Government implements a number of 
schemes and programmes to complement the efforts of the State/UTs in 
assisting the small enterprises. Such assistance may also help some small 
enterprises to grow into medium ones. 
196 

 
[1 DECEMBER, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) The SMED Bill, 2005 does not discriminate against small scale manufacturers 
nor does it contain any provision to enable medium enterprises to take away any 
benefits or incentives given to small manufacturing enterprises. 
(e) The Central Government does not think it necessary to review the concept of SME 
as proposed in the SMED Bill, 2005. 
SME Bill 
1030. PROF. R.B.S. VARMA: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Bill which was ready in 
2002, has not been passed; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons for the delay; 
(c) whether raising the investment limit to Rs. 5 crore would help only 1 per cent of 
the SSIs as 98 per cent of SSIs are less than Rs. 10 lakh worth; 
(d) the steps to be taken by Government for the benefit of SSIs with worth less 
than Rs. 10 lakh; 
(e) the reasons for which the term 'tiny' is missing form the SME Bill; 
 
(f) whether Government are not concerned with the problem of the tiny industries; 
and 
(g) the plans of Government to help the unviable and sick SSIs? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCA LE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) and (b) The Central Government approved the Small and Medium 
Enterprises Development (SMED), Bill 2005 on 4th May 2005 and the Bill was 
introduced in the Lok Sabha on 12th May 2005. There has been no delay in introducing 
the Bill in its present from. 
(c) and (d) Classification of small manufacturing enterprises, including small scale 
industries, in the SMED Bill as enterprises with investment in plant and machinery not 
exceeding Rs. 5 crore aims at helping all small enterprises, irrespective of their investment. 
The Bill seeks to extend     > benefits to all segments of small enterprises. 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [1 DECEMBER, 2005] 
(e) Clause 7(6) of the SMED Bill, 2005 clearly provides that the Central Government 
may, while classifying enterprises, include in such classification micro of tiny 
enterprises or village enterprises, as part of small enterprises. 
(f) and (g) Though the promotion and development of small scale industries, 
including tiny industry is the primary responsibility of State Governments/Union Territory 
(UTs) Administrations, the Central Government implements a number of schemes/programmes 
to complement the efforts of the States and UTs in this regard. These include, among 
others, schemes/programmes, which provide support in terms of enterpreneurship training, 
infrastructure, credit technology, marketing etc. for promotion and development of 
small scale industries. Besides, the Reserve Bank of India has issued detailed guidelines 
to commercial banks to identify potentially viable sick SSI units and take steps for 
their revival and rehabitation.

1031. SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any scheme to check sickness of small scale industries

(a) to (d) Various measures have been taken to facilitate timely identification and 
rehabilitation of potentially viable sick small scale industries (SSIs). The Reserve

of sickness at an early stage and taking remedial measures, and for rehabilitation of sick 
SSI units identified as potentially viable, these guidelines include, inter alia, change in the 
definition of sich SSI units, norms for deciding their viability, 
198 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005]        RAJYA SABHA 
concessional finance, etc., with a view to helping the banks in detecting 
sickness at an early stage and taking corrective action for revival of the 
potentially viable sick SSI units. In line with the 'Policy Package for stepping up

Government in August 2005, the RBI has further issued guidelines in

†1033. SHRI P.K. MAHESHWARI: Will the Minister of SMALL SCALE 
INDUSTRIES be pleased to state: 
(a) what is the new definition of small industries in proposed Small and 
Medium Enterprises Development Bill for the development of small and 
medium industries; 
(b) whether any concrete steps have been taken up for fully safeguarding the 
interests of small and marginal undertakings; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES (SHRI MAHABIR 
PRASAD): (a) In the Small and Medium Enterprises Development (SMED) Bill, 
2005 introduced in the Lok Sabha on 12th May 2005, a small enterprise is defined, 
in case of manufacturing enterprises, as an enterprise with investment in plant 
and machinery not exceeding 5 crore rupees and, in case of enterprises engaged 
in providing of services, as an enterprise with investment in equipment not

1037. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of STATISTICS

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION (SHRI OSCAR FERNANDES): (a) 
There is no proposal to abrogate the Member of Parliament Local Area 
Development Scheme (MPLADS) under consideration. However, MPLADS 
Guidelines have been comprehensively revised and issued on 16.11.2005. 
(b) The salient features of the revised Guidelines is given Statement (see 
below). 
(c) Since inception of the Scheme in 1993 and upto 27.11.2005, Rs. 
14350.80 crore has been released by Government of India. As per the reports 
received from the Districts as on 17.11.2005,883069 works at the cost of Rs. 
14057.68 crore had been sanctioned, out of which 780268 works have been 
completed. So far an expenditure of Rs. 12800.25 crore has been incurred. The 
percentage of utilzation over release is 89.19 and the percentage of works 
completed to works sanctioned is 88.36. 
Statement 
Revised Guidelines of MPLADS 
Member of Parliament Local Area Development Scheme (MPLADS) is under 
implementation since 1993-94. The Guidelines under the Scheme were revised 
from time to time and lastly it was revised in April, 2002. Subsequently, 
certain clarificatory circulars have been issued. Now, a comprehensive revision 
has been made and a fresh set of Guidelines has been issued on 16th November, 
2005. These Guidelines are based on the feedback received from Hon'ble MPs, the 
suggestions of the Committees on MPLADS (Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha), the 
observations made by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India and the 
operational experience gained in the monitoring of the scheme. 
206 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005]        RAJYA SABHA 
In the revised guidelines, some of the improvements are as under: 
(i) Important sectors like drinking water, education, public health, sanitation 
and roads have been given priority. 
(ii) Earmarking of funds to the extent of 15% and 7.5% funds for the development 
of SC and ST inhabited areas respectively. 
(iii) Automatic release of Rs. 1 crore in respect of MPs at the time of constitution 
of Lok Sabha and election to the Rajya Sabha without fulfilment of conditions 
including monthly progress report. 
(iv) Automatic release of first instalment in any financial year in those cases where 
two instalments have been released in the previous year. 
(v) The role of Implementing Agencies, District Authority, State Government 
and Central Government have been clearly delineated. 
(vi) Limit of Rs. 25 lakh of individual work has been removed while 
maintaining the same for Trusts/Societies/NGOs. 
(VII) List of the permissible items has been removed. Instead the list of works 
prohibited under MPLADS has been given. 
(viii) MPLADS works costing upto Rs. 10 lakh for natural calamities like floods, 
cyclone etc. by MPs from the non-affected areas of their State. 
(ix) The maximum limit for rehabilitation of work in the affected areas by severe 
calamities have been raised to Rs. 50 lakhs. 
(x) A time frame for all the works completed from 1993-94 onward has been 
prescribed for submission of Utilization Certificates and Audit Certificates. 
(xi) Utilization Certificate for the previous financial year and the Audit certificate 
for the funds utilized in the year prior to the previous year have also been 
made the pre-requisites for the release of the second instalment in a year. 
(xii) The role of Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local bodies as 
Implementing Agencies has been stressed.

THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): Thank you, Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, Sir, I am grateful to the hon. Members who have made their observations and 
sought clarifications from the statement which I laid on the Table of the House on 28th 
November. Sir, all of us agree that this is a tragic accident and of this tragic incident, all of 
us feel a little bit helpless also because what happened there and the way in which it 
happened, we did not have control over the situation. First of all, I would like to clarify one 
position, the first step Government took and how we responded to it. I would mention 
certain facts and it is true that I did not mention those facts in the original statement 
because it would have been much longer. The incident happened on 19th November at 
8.00 p.m., 20.00 hrs. Then BRO unit informed the embassy and Ambassador 
240 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
1.00 P.M. 
Rakesh Sood was contacted at 8.30. The information was that four persons have 
been kidnapped including one Indian. "Four persons" was the original information 
which was received. They were missing from the Zaranj-Delaram Highway, which is 
being constructed by the BRO. Ambassador Sood immediately contacted the 
National Security Advisor of Afghanistan, Zalari Rasool and requested him to 
immediately carry on search and investigation work. Then after contacting the 
National Security Advisor of Afghanistan, he contacted the Foreign Office here 
and the Foreign Office's Joint Secretary concerned immediately contacted the 
Cabinet Secretariat and the officer looking after Afghanistan to institute an inquiry 
through Cabinet Secretariat ch annel. This operation was on throughout the 
whole night. The BRO Unit also cont acted the Governor of Nimroz, the 
Provincial Governor of Afghanistan where this construction activity is going on. 
Next day early morning at 4.00 a.m. the Chief Security Liaison Officer working 
with the BRO, alongwith the security forces left Zaranj for searching the vehicle and 
the personnel. Then the first thing the Indian Embassy did was that they requested 
the Afghan Government for enhancing the security of the Indian companies. Our 
Ambassador continuously remained in touch with the National Security Advisor. Here 
also the Crisis Management Group in the Secretariat started functioning. The first 
information, which we got from the Reuters, was that Reuters agency in 
Kandahar received a call from one Mr. Suari Mohd. Yusuf claiming to be the 
spokesman of the Taliban and they asked for immediate suspension of construction work 
and withdrawal of the BRO personnel within 48 hours, otherwise, the hostages 
would be killed. Immediately the Ambassador contacted the office of President Karzai. 
President Karzai immediately called the Afghan Cabinet and the task force was set 
up and the task force was entrusted with the task of carrying on search and 
rescue operation. In this process the entire exercise went on. Now, certain very 
salient points have emerged. One hon. Member has asked whether we tried to 
contact the other personnel, other channels including the tribals. The answer is, 
yes. Separately our Ambassador tried and actually established contact with 
three important personnel whom he thought could help in rescuing the persons 
and at least establishing contact with the abductors. 
At that stage, from the very beginning they tried to establish contact with the 
abductors to ascertain actually what they wanted. You will have to keep in mind 
that at eight in the evening the person was abducted and the next day at 4.00 P.M. 
in the afternoon, the news was broken by Reuter that they are demanding 
withdrawal of BRO and suspension of construction 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [1 DECEMBER, 2005] 
work. So the contact which the Ambassador there established was the 
Sibgatulla Mujhadadi, former President and Foreign Head of Reconciliation 
Commission which is talking to the moderate Taliban. The second person was P. 
Gylani, head of the Qadari Sect and prominent religious leader. The third was 
Arif Moorjai, Tribal Chief and former Minister of the Tribal Affairs and all of them 
assured that they tried to establish contact with the abductors and tried to help. 
Here, the Prime Minister took the meeting himself with the concerned officers and 
directed that every effort should be made to ensure that the person concerned is 
rescued and the family members are also contacted. BRO officials remained in 
constant touch with the family members. The group which was set up—I would not 
like to go to all the details, that is the normal practice—they constantly monitored the 
situation, in addition to contacting the Afghan Government, constantly being in 
touch with the national security advisor of Afghanistan, being in touch with the 
office of the President and personally talking to the President. Afghan Cabinet met 
twice to assess the situation and do their best. Our Ambassador contacted the 
Iranian Ambassador, the US Ambassador and also the Italian Ambassador there 
because Italy being the current head of the international security force delployed 
in Afghanistan. So all these contacts were established and efforts were made. It 
is not correct to say that efforts were no made. Now, these exercises continued 
from 18th night till 21st. Then Mr. Jaswant Singh said, 'why was there a 
difference between MEA statement and my statement'? There were two news. 
The first news came that some news agency visited the call allegedly from 
Taliban claiming that the Indian hostage has been killed. But still, as the hon.

having, "no direct contact', none of the parties concerned was able to establish 
direct contact with the abductors in the Taliban. All these contacts which were

channels which was received said that 'no, it is not confirmed.' Later on, the next 
day when the body was found, naturally, there was no question of having any doubt 
and thereafter the whole thing was done and this is the effort which was made. So,

Concern over variation in Drug Prices in the Country 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I would like to start 
my Special Mention by giving an example about the variation in the amount spent 
by two patients to treat the high blood pressure with exactly the same medicine 
and dose. 
One has been prescribed the Amlodac brand of amlodipine that costs Rs. 550 
per year. While another spends four times more, i.e., Rs. 2200, as his doctor 
has. prescribed a more expensive brand Amlogard. 
Both these brands are marketed by top quality reputed pharma 
manufacturers. 
Is it fair? Should such a state of affairs continue? 
Sir, hundreds of similar cases exist, with two brands of the same medicine 
being priced very differently. 
Indian pharma companies annually spend over Rs. 5340 crore to promote their 
brands to the medical profession. That is around Rs. 1,33,000 per doctor per 
year. That whole cost, needless to say, is recovered from the patients. 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [1 DECEMBER, 2005] 
Hence, the Government should propose that the doctors should be made to 
prescribe all single ingredient medicines by their chemical names, which is a step in 
the right direction. It will enable the patients to compare prices and purchase the 
least expensive product. 
The Government must also simultaneously take several other steps for the 
successful implementation of this proposal. 
It must, first of all, make it mandatory for pharma producers to use chemical 
names instead of brand names for all single ingredient medicines. Thank you, Sir. 
Demand for Additional Air Tonnage for carrying out Ration 
Sorties by Indian Air Force, Helicopters in Arunachal Pradesh 
SHRI NABAM REBIA (Arunachal Pradesh):  Sir, as on date, there are 18 
numbers of air-fed locations in remote/international border areas of this border 
State, inaccessible by surface communication. One has to walk for days 
together through difficult porter tract to reach such air-fed administrative centres. 
Air sorties are the only means to dispatch essential commodities for Government 
employees, students and the paramilitary forces deployed there, as there is no 
sufficient crop production or proper marketing facilities. 
Out of the projected annual requirem ent of air tonnage of 3150 MT (1300 
MT in Fixed Wing and 1850 MT in Rotary Wing) for the year 2005-06, the 
Ministry of Defence has so far allotted only 1400 MT (900 MT in Fixed Wing 
and 500 MT in Rotary Wing), which is quite insufficient. The allotted 500 MT 
in Rotary Wing has already been exhausted and the 14 air fed administrative 
centres (out of 18 numbers) feasible for Rotary Wing operation are facing acute 
hardship and utter starvation. 
It is requested to organize the required additional air tonnage in Rotary Wing to 
avert any report of starvation death and law and order problem in this remote 
border State. 
Concern over deletion of names from the electoral rolls in Goa 
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, the process of preparation of 
electoral rolls is on in the country. However, the concept of 'ordinary resident' 
is misinterpreted by the election authori ties engaged in the preparation of 
electoral rolls. 
248 

[1 DECEMBER, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
It is well-known that lakhs of Indians, especially those coming from States 
like Goa and Kerala, are working on board the ships as also in the gulf countries. 
During summary revision of the electoral rolls held in the last two years, 
thousands of names of voters working on board the ships and in gulf countries 
were deleted from the electoral rolls in Goa. In fact, those who work on board 
the ships and in the gulf countries go there temporarily and they come to their 
respective States every two years or so. If elections to Parliament, Assembly or 
local bodies are held during their stay in their home State, they should be 
entitled to participate. 
An amendment to the Representation of People's Act, therefore, is the need of 
the hour, to clear the confusion resulting from denial of the prestigious right to 
vote to this class of voters. Just because they remain absent temporarily from 
their respective houses with other members of the family very much residing in 
the house, they should not be deprived of their right to vote.

Demand to ban the sale of clothing items similar to Military                                    
and police uniforms in the country 
DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, anti-social elements like 
thieves, dacoits, etc. and anti-national elements like terrorists and others, 
generally strike in the guise of military or police personnel, wearing clothing items 
similar to military or police uniform, to carry out their nefarious activities and spread 
terror and bloodshed by killing the innocents or looting or robbing the unsuspecting 
citizens. But, unfortunately, clothing items similar to military and police 
uniforms, their badges, belts, shoes and even medals are available for sale at 
throwaway prices in the open market. In the national capital itself these items are 
available in plenty in the Chandni Chowk area and anybody can purchase them for a 
pittance. The terrorists and anti-social elements are using these uniforms with 
impunity to impersonate as military or police personnel. 
Of course, there are provisions in the Indian Penal Code and Official Secrets 
Act to prevent the misuse of such uniforms, but these provisions are applicable 
after the offence is committed. But where will one find the terrorists to try under 
these provisions of law? Hence to prevent the misuse of clothing items similar to 
military and police uniforms, badges, medals, etc., a blanket ban has to be 
imposed throughout the country and wide publicity to such a ban has to be 
carried out through print and electronic media. Non-availability of such uniforms 
will, at least, hamper their misuse though their misuse cannot be totally ruled 
out. 
I, therefore, demand that Central Government should through notification ban the 
sale of clothing items similar to milit ary or police uniforms and their badges, 
medals, etc., in the open market throughout the country with immediate effect.

Metro Rail 
SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I 
stand here to draw the attention of the Ministry of Railways to the problems of daily 
commuters of Kolkata Metro Railways. The air-conditioning machines installed at 
Central, Chandni Chowk, Mahatma G andhi Road, Girish Park, Shovabazar, 
Shyambazar and Belgachia North stations are not working for the last one year. Naturally 
the commuters feel unprecedented humid conditions in the underground stations. When the 
Metro Railways were constructed, the IIT, Kharagpur engineers stressed on continuous 
operation of air-conditioning and ventilation systems. The drawings, prepared by IIT have 
been destroyed long ago. As a result, Metro authorities are using pedestal fans which 
are inadequate to maintain equilibrium between oxygen and carbon dioxide in the 
underground tunnel. Apart from that, the escalators, installed at Central station are 
not working properly. Of and on, the commuters are to use the stairs instead of the 
escalator. In the Park Street station, commuters are compelled to use steep 
staircases as there is no escalator. I demand immediate intervention of the Ministry of 
Railways to resolve the problems of the commuters of Kolkata Metro Railways.

Concern over shortage of revenue stamps in the country,                           
particularly in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. Deputy Chairman, 
Sir, revenue stamp is one of the sources of revenue to the Government. In 
transactions in excess of Rs. 500 and on the negotiable instruments, it is required 
to have the necessary value of revenue stamp for legal authenticity. During the 
last four to five years, there has been  severe shortage of revenue stamps in 
the country, causing a lot of inconvenience to the people and revenue losses 
to the Government exchequer. 
For example, the Government of Andhra Pradesh indented for supply of stamps 
worth Rs. 126 crores from Indian Security Press but was supplied stamps worth 
Rs. 10.9 crores only. For an order of Court Fee labels for Rs. 16 crores, supply 
was to the tune of Rs. 2.26 crores only. I understand that the LIC has also started 
issuing receipts on payments receiv ed without revenue,stamp. Unstamped 
documents, with mere provisional signatures in lieu of revenue stamps, have 
become a source of tension for the people. This clearly shows the magnitude of the 
problems in the country. Now, the Postal Department is adding fuel to fire. Till 
now, the post offices are selling reve nue stamps. Now, the Post Master 
General of Punjab has decided to stop selling revenue stamps through post 
offices saying that the Union Communications Ministry has directed the postal 
department to charge 3 per cent commission from district treasury in lieu of 
revenue stamps collected and sold in post offices. This has further aggravated the 
problem. Hence, I request the Government of India to take measures 
immediately and see that sufficient rev enue stamps are available in all post 
offices. I also request the Communications Ministry to help the States in installing 
franking machines in sub-registrar offices and should also allow banks, 
insurance companies to use franking machines for their needs.

of The Constitution of India 
SHRI B. K. HARIPRASAD (Karnataka): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I would 
like to draw the attention of the Government towards the Karnataka Act 24 of 2004, 
on admission to medical, dental and engineering courses, and, the plea for

education to students from all over India, is now confronted with a flurry of

Demand to Explore Ways and Means to Tackle Naxalite Menace 
in Orissa 
MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR (Orissa): Sir, Orissa is treated as an island of 
peace amidst various types of violence in the surrounding States. But, in the 
recent past, the menace of Maoist and Naxalite violence has reared its head in 
Orissa also. According to  reports, the extremist groups in Jharkhand, 
Chhattisgarh and Andhra Pradesh are trying to open a corridor through the 
districts of Sundergarh, Deogarh and Sambalpur for easy passage. 
In some recent incidents, lives of i nnocent civilians in some villages of 
Sambalpur have been lost, including that of police personnel. As such, the 
Southern District of Malkangiri, Gajpati and Raigarh are facing violent incidents 
of Naxalites for quite some time. Even the house of a former Minister of Orissa 
was blown up in Malkangiri district last month. 
There is a general perception that this is a law and order problem and should 
be handled by the respective State Govern ments. But, it is not limited to that 
alone. Economic deprivation, regional imbalance, lack of employment avenues, 
lack of purposeful engagement of the rural and tribal

Atrocities against women in Delhi 
DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA (Rajasthan): Sir, the caption of my Special 
Mention is 'Alarming scenario of atrocities against women in Delhi'. 
In the National Capital of Delhi, alarming rise in the atrocities against women 
is a matter of national concern. As against 3870 such cases reported in the year 
2001,4106 cases were reported in the year 2002,4338 cases

RAJYA SABHA [1 DECEMBER, 2005] 
were reported in the year 2003 and 5568 cases were reported in the year 2004 
which indicates a rising trend in Delhi. According to the National Crime Record 
Bureau, Delhi alone had recorded more than 30 per cent of total cases of 
atrocities committed against women in 35 metropolitan cities of the country 
during the year 2003. During 2004, total rapes reported in Delhi were 551, which 
means one rape is committed every 16 hours, while the average for India is one 
rape is committed every 32 hours. 
 
Thus, rape rate in the capital is double than the national average. Per ten lakh 
population, Delhi reports 36 rapes as against India average of 16 rapes. It is a 
matter of grave anxiety and shame that out of 551 rape cases in 2004, 317 victims 
were minor girls, and 14 of the accused were fathers and 527 were 
acquaintances. In famous case of a Swiss diplomat, who was abducted at Siri 
Fort and gang-raped in a moving car on 14th October 2003, was a national shame. 
She left Delhi exclaiming, 'India is not safe for women'. Similar gang-rapes were 
committed in 2005 — on 5th May at Dhoulan Kuan, on 20th July at Mayapuri, on 
24th July in Rohini, and on 10th August at Najafgarh. Many of the rape cases have 
remained unsolved. Conviction rate is abysmally poor. It appears that Delhi is 
going to earn honorific of 'Rape Capital of India.' I, therefore, demand that the 
Government take effective steps to redress the problem, which is bringing shame 
to the country.

SHRIMATI BRINDA KARAT (West Bengal): Sir, my Special Mention relates 
to the concern over violation of civil li berties due to non-implementation of the 
POTA Central Review Committee's recommendations. 
Sir, a very important issue of civil liberties has arisen regarding the plight of 
those held under POTA. As the provisions of POTA allowed room for grave 
misuse, the law was scrapped. However, the injustices remain. The matter 
requires urgent intervention in the light of the refusal of relevant authorities to 
implement the recommendations of the POTA Central Review Committee which 
has held that there is not sufficient evidence against many of those held under 
POTA and that they should be released. Yet the persons languish in jails. This 
includes 85 persons held in the terrible

in other cases, the perpetrators of communal genocide who have been identified are not

SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE (Assam): Sir, Assam grows 53% of India's total tea. 
India being the world's largest producer and the fourth largest exporter of tea, Assam is

competition from Sri Lanka and other countries. The labour unrest has been 
mostly the result of the economic fall-out-and it further compounds the problem. 
Another predicament in industry is that most of the tea companies in Assam 
are not registered in the State and collateral benefit of their profitability in the form 
of share of Central taxes is denied to Assam. There are Some popular tea brands 
which control about two-thirds of India's tea market. They have their registered offices

taxes that they pay accrue to West Bengal which affects the State's economy.

plucking and cultivation. Big brokers, in addition to evaluation of tea, also fix tea

Lankan tea having an edge on consumer preference does not augur well for the 
tea industry, half of which is grown in Assam.

Menace of Tobacco in the Country 
SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI (Nominated): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
draw the kind attention of the Government towards the menace of tobacco. 
The then Prime Minister inaugurated the International Conference on 'Global 
Tobacco Control Law' in 2000, promising an exhaustive law to discour age 
smoking and chewing of tobacco. 
As stated by the then Secretary, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, a draft 
Bill is ready. And also the hon. Minister of Health and Family Welfare assured of an 
effective law on the subject. 
263 

RAJYA SA8HA [1 DECEMBER, 2005] 
Everyday, 2,400 Indian citizens die of tobacco consumption. In urban areas, 24 percent 
male and in rural areas, 35 per cent male and 4 to 8 per cent female are addicted to tobacco 
and it preparations. 
Tobacco causes eye irritation, headache, cough, sore throat, dizziness, nausea, decline in 
lung function, asthma in children, cancer, chronic lung disease by which the country loses 
Rs. 30,000 crores a year. 
Smoking during pregnancy is responsible for low birth rate and there is higher rate of 
miscarriage and neo-natal death. 
Those children whose parents are smokers or tobacco addicts, become victims of bronchitis, 
respiratory systems, lung cancer and other diseases. Even passive smoking has all toxic 
components. So the presence of an individual near a smoker is also dangerous. 
Tobacco is more dangerous than the Kargil War, the Tsunami disaster, cyclones and 
earthquakes. 
Tobacco farming earns only Rs. 12,000 crores a year, but nearly two lakh cancer 
patients require a staggering sum of Rs. 700 crores for their medical treatment. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Government to discourage the use of tobacco and its 
preparations, by law, as promised five years back. Thank you.
